topics: al-Qurʾān and al-Furqān as gathering and separation
The basmalah as an āyah of al-Fātiḥah
The pre-eternity of the divine names
body: Shaykh Ibrāhīm opens with the principles of tafsīr, which explains the speech of Allah by transmission. Taʾwīl shows by reason that the words can bear a meaning, and reason is accepted where no report from the Prophet ﷺ exists. The exegete needs the speech of the Arabs, the rulings of the sharīʿah, bayān and badīʿ, and a light in the heart. He reads Q. 75:16–19 as three promises Allah has kept: the Qurʾan's gathering, recitation and clarification. He reduces its fifty-five names to al-Qurʾān and al-Furqān, gathering and separation: without separation the servant has no servanthood, and without gathering he has no recognition (maʿrifah).

Rūḥ al-bayān records the objection that seeking refuge from Satan shows fear of other than Allah and impairs servanthood. Shaykh Ibrāhīm recasts it as a question of recognition and answers that the istiʿādhah is courtesy (adab) toward Allah. One whose station is not to see Satan needs no refuge.

The Jalālayn leaves open whether the basmalah is part of al-Fātiḥah. Shaykh Ibrāhīm sides with al-Shāfiʿī and gives two of al-Rāzī's proofs: the basmalah is written in the muṣḥaf in the script of the Qurʾan, and the earlier prophets, whom the Prophet ﷺ was told to follow (Q. 6:90), began with Allah's name. Al-Qurṭubī, for Mālik, answers that it may mark the division of the surahs, citing a version of Shaykh Ibrāhīm's report. With al-Qurṭubī he derives ism from sumuww and rejects the Muʿtazilī view that Allah had no name before creation: Allah named Himself al-Raḥmān and al-Ghafūr before any creature needed mercy or pardon, which strengthens the servant's hope. With al-Ṣāwī and al-Rāzī, against al-Zamakhsharī, he holds that the name Allah is underived.

He lists the names and virtues of al-Fātiḥah and reads the surah as a summary of the nine genres of the Qurʾan. On Q. 2:2–5 he follows Rūḥ al-bayān in giving the four descriptions of the believers to the four caliphs. At Q. 2:4 he adds that one who believes in all the saints but rejects the perfect one of his age is cut off from Allah, as one who rejects the prophet of his time is an unbeliever. The commentaries he worked from draw no such analogy here. Ḥaqqī draws one at Q. 27:40. He closes on the virtue of spending.
1.author: A.K.

topics: The meaning and kinds of kufr
Abū Ṭālib and recognition of the truth
The zunnār as a mark of kufr
Divine knowledge and the Prophet's hope
body: On Q. 2:6 Shaykh Ibrāhīm works closely from Ismāʿīl Ḥaqqī's Rūḥ al-bayān. He defines kufr lexically as covering over and legally as denying what the Prophet ﷺ is known by necessity to have brought. He gives Ḥaqqī's four senses of kāfir in the Qurʾan and the four kinds of kufr Ḥaqqī takes from al-Baghawī, among them the kufr of Abū Ṭālib, who affirmed in verse the truth of Muḥammad's religion but did not take Islam as his own. Ḥaqqī and al-Rāzī treat tying on the zunnār as evidence that a man does not assent, not as kufr in itself. Ḥaqqī adds that, unlike fornication and wine, nothing draws a man to it. Shaykh Ibrāhīm keeps both points and concludes that the man who ties it makes light of Islam and is an unbeliever. With the Jalālayn he reads Q. 2:6 as cutting off the Prophet's hope, and with Ḥaqqī he contrasts Nūḥ, who learned the same only after long hardship and then prayed for his people's destruction. He adds that the Prophet ﷺ, sent as a mercy (Q. 21:107), did not pray against his people.

On the hypocrites he retells, without names, al-Rāzī's report of al-Kindī asking al-Mubarrad about three degrees of emphasis. He applies it to Q. 2:8 with al-Rāzī and al-Ṣāwī: the hypocrites claimed āmannā in the verbal form, and Allah answered with the nominal wa-mā hum bi-muʾminīn, which removes them from the body of the believers.

With al-Rāzī's permutations of k-l-m he shows that the Arabs heard meaning in every Qurʾanic word, yet could make nothing of the disconnected letters. With a report in Rūḥ al-bayān he holds that the Prophet ﷺ recognized Kāf Hā Yā ʿAyn Ṣād before Jibrīl did.

He explains establishing the prayer. On Q. 2:21 he accepts the Jalālayn's rule that laʿalla in Allah's speech expresses certainty, then reads it from the servant's side as hope. Al-Rāzī calls that reading a taʾwīl. Shaykh Ibrāhīm says it needs none. He gives Ḥaqqī's ten kinds of the self-deluded and three degrees of shirk. He traces the challenge from the whole Qurʾan to ten surahs to one, and cites Musaylimah's imitation of al-Kawthar and an imitation of al-Fātiḥah commissioned by the Americans. He closes with the rivers, fruits and spouses of the Garden.
2.author: A.K.

body: Shaykh Ibrāhīm opens with the occasion of revelation of Q. 2:26: the Jews objected that the parables of the fly and the spider were beneath Allah. Where the Jalālayn glosses the shame as not omitting to explain, and al-Ṣāwī calls it a trope, he applies al-Rāzī's canon: every attribute impossible of Allah has a beginning, which is impossible of Him, and an end, which is admissible. Shame begins as shrinking from blame and ends in leaving the act. Only the leaving applies to Allah. He names the three covenants that al-Bayḍāwī and Rūḥ al-bayān list, but makes the prophets' covenant the pledge of Q. 3:81 to believe in and follow Muḥammad. Al-Rāzī cites the ahl al-ibāḥah at Q. 2:29 and refutes them. Shaykh Ibrāhīm answers them by grammar: the lām of "for you" marks entitlement, not licence.

The angels foresaw corruption in Ādam's constitution: of al-Ṣāwī's three powers, anger and appetite must overcome intellect. Or they learned it from the word khilāfah or from the Preserved Tablet, two of al-Rāzī's explanations. Ādam's knowledge of the names won him the vicegerency, and from this the scholars infer that only one who knows may lead. He names seven people Allah taught directly and cites ʿAlī on seven ways knowledge surpasses wealth.

Iblīs's questions, which reason cannot answer, reach him through al-Rāzī's report of al-Shahrastānī. With al-Shahrastānī he traces every later sect's doubt back to them. Ādam repented with words received from his Lord and was accepted. Iblīs repented with words of his own and was not. Al-Ṣāwī draws the shaykh's authorization (idhn) from those words, and reads the eating as forbidden outwardly but not inwardly. Shaykh Ibrāhīm adds the intimate address in which Ādam consents to appear disobedient, and calls the act disobedience in form and obedience in reality, citing Ibn al-ʿArabī and al-Jīlī as al-Ṣāwī does. Q. 20:121 stands as Allah's word. Ādam's sons owe their father dutifulness. Against the Jalālayn's "abiding forever", he takes khulūd as long remaining, with the argument from abadan that al-Bayḍāwī and al-Rāzī make.

From Q. 2:40 he turns to the Children of Isrāʾīl: Firʿawn's slaughter of their sons, Mūsā's forty-day fast as the basis of the forty-day khalwah, ḥiṭṭah as lā ilāha illā Llāh, and the wilderness, where blessing and punishment alike came through companionship.
3.author: A.K.

topics: The twelve springs and the senses
Friday and the hour of answered prayer
body: On Mūsā's rock (Q. 2:60) Shaykh Ibrāhīm holds, with Ismāʿīl Ḥaqqī's Rūḥ al-bayān, that earlier communities brought their requests to Allah through their prophets, while this ummah may ask Him directly. From the Taʾwīlāt najmiyyah that Ḥaqqī quotes, he reads the twelve springs as twelve senses, five outward, five inward, the nafs and the heart, that flow when the rock of the servant's existence is struck with lā ilāha illā Llāh. He rewrites their drinking places: where the Taʾwīlāt give the nafs its appetites, he gives it worship and striving.

Q. 2:61–66 bring the demand for the earth's produce, the killing of prophets, the raised Mount and the Sabbath-breakers. The Qurʾan is silent on those who neither fished nor forbade it. Against ʿIkrima's view that they were saved, with which the Jalālayn ends and which al-Rāzī defends, he holds with Ibn ʿAbbās's first view that they perished, citing Q. 5:79. He places the hour of answered prayer at the end of Friday, with ʿAbd Allāh b. Salām, for one who sits in remembrance awaiting the sunset prayer, a practice he calls particular to the Tijānīs. The commentators read "Be apes" (Q. 2:65) as a creative command. He reads it as an imperative of belittlement and lists thirteen of a promised fifteen senses, most with al-Juwaynī's examples but not always his labels.

After the cow and the youth devoted to his mother, he reads the hardened hearts of Q. 2:74 as grounds for remembering Allah aloud and in company: many strikers break stone sooner. Against the commentator's Torah reading of Q. 2:75 and al-Rāzī's preference, he applies the āyah, with al-Ṭabarī, to those who heard Allah speak to Mūsā. Rūḥ al-bayān rejects that reading.

In Q. 2:81–82, as al-Ṣāwī notes, a fāʾ of causation ties the Fire to the unbeliever's doing, while no fāʾ ties the Garden to deeds. With Ḥaqqī he makes intention the ground of eternal abiding, and with al-Rāzī argues that no finite deed earns an eternity. He ties Q. 2:84–85 to the Aws, Khazraj, Qurayẓah and Naḍīr, and Q. 2:97 to Ibn Ṣūriyā's questions. On Hārūt and Mārūt, where the Jalālayn says that whoever learns sorcery disbelieves, he holds that teaching evil is obligatory so that it may be avoided, much as al-Rāzī makes knowing it obligatory.
4.author: A.K.

topics: "There is no bequest to an heir"
The face of Allah and the qiblah
"Do not prefer me over Yūnus b. Mattā"
The ten builders of the Kaʿbah
body: Shaykh Ibrāhīm opens with Q. 2:106. The Jews and the polytheists held that abrogated speech cannot be the speech of Allah. He answers that transmission establishes abrogation and reason accepts it, since Allah disposes of His rulings as He wills. His three forms of abrogation, with their three examples, are al-Ṣāwī's. On the third, the āyah of bequest (Q. 2:180), he parts from the Jalālayn and al-Ṣāwī, which make the hadith "There is no bequest to an heir" a second abrogator beside the āyah of inheritance, and from al-Qurṭubī, who makes the Sunnah the abrogator and finds this in Mālik's rulings. He holds that the hadith only makes the abrogation clear, because the speech of a creature is never better than the speech of the Creator. Al-Rāzī and al-Khāzin report this argument as al-Shāfiʿī's.

He tells the story of Hārūt and Mārūt in al-Ṣāwī's frame and rejects it: the exegetes took it from the Isrāʾīliyyāt alone, and the Qurʾan gives it the lie. Al-Ṣāwī leaves the question open between Ibn Ḥajar, who accepts the story, and al-Bayḍāwī, who rejects it. Al-Rāzī and al-Qurṭubī reject it outright. A tale of an envious courtier shows envy recoiling on the envier.

At Q. 2:115 he takes the Jalālayn's gloss of "the face of Allah", "His qiblah which He approved", and adds the reading al-Ṣāwī assigns to the Sufis: the face is the Essence, which has no direction. Al-Ṣāwī quotes Ibn al-ʿArabī that facing one qiblah is pure worship whose reason we do not grasp. Shaykh Ibrāhīm gives the reason: facing one direction outwardly trains the inward to face the real qiblah. From Rūḥ al-bayān at this āyah he takes the tale of Imām al-Ḥaramayn and the poor man's debt, leaves the scholar unnamed, and turns the question to "Do not prefer me over Yūnus b. Mattā". His answer is the reading al-Qurṭubī records from al-Juwaynī himself: Muḥammad ﷺ beyond the heavens is no nearer to Allah than Yūnus at the bottom of the sea.

Ibrāhīm's trial leads to the ten builders of the Kaʿbah, Hājar and Zamzam, Ismāʿīl's two wives, and Rābiʿah's rebuke of al-Junayd. After Bahlūl admonishes Hārūn al-Rashīd come the change of qiblah, the ummah's testimony for Nūḥ, and the rulings on retaliation, bequests, fasting and hajj, ending at Q. 2:202.
5.author: A.K.

topics: Annihilation in the acts, the attributes and the Essence
body: Shaykh Ibrāhīm opens with the numbered days of Q. 2:203, which the Jalālayn glosses as the three days of tashrīq. He reports al-Shāfiʿī's argument, also in al-Rāzī, that the clause on hastening makes the numbered days the days of stoning. From al-Ṣāwī he takes Mālik's reckoning of four days, some "numbered", some "known" (Q. 22:28), some both. Whether he hastens or delays, the pilgrim in reality is the one mindful of Allah.

Counting from Q. 2:200, he names four kinds of people. The hypocrite who sold his Hereafter for this world is al-Akhnas b. Sharīq. Ṣuhayb al-Rūmī, who gave up his property to emigrate, sold this world for his Hereafter. Rūḥ al-bayān sets out a ladder here: giving up property, then children, then the self, discloses the unity of the acts, of the attributes and of the Essence. He keeps the ladder and names its rungs annihilation in the acts, the attributes and the Essence.

At Q. 2:208 he follows the Jalālayn's occasion: ʿAbd Allāh b. Salām and his companions kept the Sabbath after Islam. Rūḥ al-bayān has the Prophet ﷺ tell them to leave what they were used to. He carries that rebuke of custom into his own day: whoever upholds racial division defies "The believers are only brothers" (Q. 49:10). He distinguishes two emigrations and two jihads and traces the prohibition of wine through four āyāt.

Al-Ṣāwī calls the widow's four months and ten (Q. 2:234) pure worship with no reason we grasp, and rejects the explanation from the movement of the fetus. Shaykh Ibrāhīm gives that explanation. The three forties of the embryo answer to the three forties of Ādam's creation, and the added ten days, as in Rūḥ al-bayān, let a faint movement grow strong enough to reveal a pregnancy.

The Jalālayn lists the views on the middle prayer without choosing. Al-Ṣāwī assigns the dawn prayer to Mālik and the afternoon prayer to al-Shāfiʿī. Al-Qurṭubī holds that the evidence leaves it undetermined. Shaykh Ibrāhīm, a Mālikī, judges the afternoon prayer the strongest view, as al-Ṭabarī did, because the sound hadith of the Trench names it. Allah concealed it, as He concealed the Night of Decree, so that the servant keeps all five. The lesson ends with Ṭālūt, the Ark and Dāwūd's killing of Jālūt (Q. 2:252).
6.author: A.K.

topics: The four birds and the seven gates of Hell
The four parts of the Qurʾan
The hand of Allah and the mutashābih
The chief qadi of the Hijaz
body: Shaykh Ibrāhīm opens with Q. 2:253 and turns the Jalālayn's gloss on the Prophet's raised degrees into proof that he excels all the prophets. His grounds come from al-Rāzī: Allah sent him as a mercy to all the worlds, joined obedience to him with obedience to Himself, raised his renown and sealed prophethood with him, and the challenge by a surah as short as al-Kawthar makes every three āyāt a miracle. He drops the objections al-Rāzī weighs and declares that whoever doubts this excellence has left the religion. For the ḥabīb over the khalīl he uses three of the verse-pairs that al-Qāḍī ʿIyāḍ's al-Shifāʾ reports from Ibn Fūrak: Ibrāhīm asked for forgiveness and lasting praise, and Muḥammad ﷺ received both unasked.

Rūḥ al-bayān supplies the seventeen mentions of Allah in Āyat al-Kursī and the three formulas of tawḥīd: the generality say "There is no deity but He", the elect "There is no deity but You", and those who pass away from themselves hear "There is no deity but I". From its comments on Q. 3:191 and Q. 28:30 he brings in the husk, kernel and oil, the formula read as no one worshipped, no one sought and nothing existent but Allah, and the tree that spoke to Mūsā.

With al-Rāzī and Rūḥ al-bayān he finds no adab in ʿUzayr's question, which al-Ṣāwī only clears of doubt, and full adab in Ibrāhīm's. The four birds carry the dispositions al-Ṣāwī assigns them: lust, covetousness, gluttony and vainglory. The seven vices born of the four elements, the seven gates of Hell, come from al-Taʾwīlāt al-najmiyyah as Rūḥ al-bayān quotes it.

At Q. 3:7 he adapts al-Ṣāwī's fourfold division of the Qurʾan from Ibn ʿAbbās, but leaves the mutashābih to the part known to Allah alone. Against reading the hand as power he cites the objection al-Rāzī records: power takes no dual. He equally rejects the claim of the chief qadi of the Hijaz that Allah sits on the Throne: we do not find Allah in His House, he replied, and cannot say how the livestock "descended" from heaven. He settles on al-Shāfiʿī's formula, also transmitted by Ibn Qudāmah: we believe in what Allah said according to what Allah intended. The lesson ends with Badr and the seven desires of Q. 3:14.
7.author: A.K.

topics: The sensory and the spiritual Garden
The lesser and the greater walāyah
"As you are, so will you be governed"
Love of Allah and following the Prophet ﷺ
The parents' state and the child
body: At Q. 3:15 the Garden is two gardens, sensory and spiritual, as in Rūḥ al-bayān, and the spiritual garden is recognition of Allah. Some work from fear of the Fire, some from desire for the Garden, and the free work for the face of Allah. Rūḥ al-bayān gives the hadith of three, six and nine hundred degrees for three kinds of patience. With al-Ṣāwī at Q. 3:200, Shaykh Ibrāhīm ranks abstaining from disobedience highest, and only the virtuous reach it. Al-Ṣāwī and Rūḥ al-bayān read the wāw between the attributes of Q. 3:17 as making each praiseworthy alone. From that wāw he draws a lesser walāyah, open to anyone with one praised attribute, beneath the greater walāyah of the recognizers, a step that the Jalālayn, al-Ṣāwī, Rūḥ al-bayān, al-Rāzī, al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Khāzin and Ibn ʿAjībah do not take.

Allah has no direction, place or time, so the descent of the hadith is His turning toward the servant with mercy, the metaphor Rūḥ al-bayān offers. In Lesson 7 he told the qadi of the Hijaz that he cannot know how Allah descends. Here he says what the descent means. At Q. 3:26 he reads the Jalālayn's "by Your power" for "in Your hand" unremarked, a gloss al-Ṣāwī calls the khalaf's taʾwīl.

Ghālib al-Qaṭṭān waits a year for al-Aʿmash's hadith of the testimony deposited with Allah. "As you are, so will you be governed" sets the best over an obedient people. At Q. 3:28 he drops the Jalālayn's limit on taqiyyah, "before Islam grew strong". Allying with the tongue under an unbeliever's power is a dispensation. The firm course, as al-Rāzī also holds, refuses even that. Q. 3:31 makes following the Prophet ﷺ the proof of love for Allah.

Maryam's fruit out of season is a saint's karāmah, and whoever denies the karāmāt belies two hundred āyāt and more than five hundred hadith. Rūḥ al-bayān draws the same proof and ascribes the irhāṣ reading to the deniers. The lesson reports it right after them. With Rūḥ al-bayān he holds that the parents' food and intention shape the child, and adds lawful marriage and creed. Zakariyyāʾ's aspiration made Yaḥyā chaste, and Jibrīl's breath gave ʿĪsā angelic states. He closes with the mubāhalah with Najrān and the covenant of the prophets (Q. 3:81).
8.author: A.K.

topics: The wayfarer between angel and animal
Division in doctrine and in law
body: Shaykh Ibrāhīm opens with Q. 3:92: spend from what you love. Abū Ṭalḥah gives away Bayraḥāʾ, Ibn ʿUmar distributes the almonds with sugar he loves, ʿUmar b. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz frees a slave girl he desired, and Fuḍayl hands a beggar the chicken he craved. Ḥaqqī's Rūḥ al-bayān tells of Abū Ṭalḥah and ʿUmar b. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, gives the sugar and the chicken to al-Rabīʿ, and supplies al-Qushayrī's saying, which Shaykh Ibrāhīm restates: piety (al-birr) comes from giving part of what one owns. Al-Barr, who is Allah, is found only by giving everything, as Ibrāhīm did.

He traces the ban on camel meat and milk (Q. 3:93) to Yaʿqūb's vow and reads Q. 3:93–95 as a guide for the wayfarer, who can rise above the angel or sink below the cattle. On Q. 3:96 the Jalālayn puts forty years between the angels' building of the Kaʿbah and al-Aqṣā. He calls it a slip of the pen and, with al-Ṣāwī, puts the forty years between Ādam's building of the Kaʿbah and his building of al-Aqṣā. The angels built the Kaʿbah two thousand years before Ādam.

On Q. 3:102 he reads the Jalālayn's report that Q. 64:16 abrogated the āyah, then the reply in al-Rāzī's and al-Khāzin's words: whoever fears Allah as much as he is able has feared Him as He ought to be feared. His three degrees of godfearing match Ḥaqqī's at Q. 2:2: the commons believe and obey, the elect keep the Jalālayn's gloss, and in the elect of the elect nothing but Allah crosses the mind, as in Ibn al-Fāriḍ's line, which al-Ṣāwī quotes. To the Jalālayn's "His religion" he adds Ibn Masʿūd's reading of "the rope of Allah": the community. Like al-Qurṭubī, he forbids division in doctrine and enmity, not disagreement in law, in which the Companions differed sharply without enmity. On Q. 3:104 he keeps the Jalālayn's partitive min and its bar on the ignorant, and adds two conditions: standing, and no worse wrong in forbidding.

From Q. 3:121 he narrates Badr and Uḥud: the consultation, the archers who left their post, and Iblīs's cry that Muḥammad had been killed. He permits incantation by the Qurʾan, the divine names and intelligible Arabic supplication, and closes with the martyrs alive with their Lord (Q. 3:169–170).
9.author: A.K.

topics: Reflection on creation and on the Essence
Five things the seeker of the Garden must hold
Orphans and the age of majority
body: Shaykh Ibrāhīm resumes at Q. 3:171 with the forms of martyrdom. He explains "Allah is sufficient for us" (Q. 3:173) through Ibrāhīm in the fire, who told Jibrīl that Allah's knowledge of his state spared him from asking. He distinguishes the lesser jihad of the sword from the greater jihad against the nafs. Q. 3:182 denies that Allah is ẓallām. Al-Ṣāwī reads the form as attribution, not intensity. Shaykh Ibrāhīm takes it as an intensive and answers with the reason Ḥaqqī gives at Q. 8:51 and al-Bayḍāwī at Q. 22:10: created beings are so many that any wrong toward them would make the wrongdoer ẓallām.

Under Q. 3:185 a devotee sets this world's seven thousand years against the fifty thousand of the Day of Resurrection. Praise destroys one kind of person, sends the elect back to Allah in humility, and reaches the perfected as praise from Allah. ʿĀʾishah's account of the Prophet ﷺ weeping over Q. 3:191 brings him to reflection, which the Jalālayn limits to inferring the Maker from creation. Ḥaqqī, al-Qurṭubī and al-Rāzī cite "reflect on the creation, not on the Creator". Shaykh Ibrāhīm leaves that inference to the commons, forbids them reflection on the Essence because they would picture a body, and grants it to the elect. He lists five things the seeker of the Garden must hold to, and tells of a walī turned away from a bathhouse, al-Ḥaddād whom fire does not burn, and a youth who escapes a seduction.

He opens Sūrat al-Nisāʾ with the single soul and the ties of kinship, then treats orphans' property, polygyny, dowers and the shares. To the Jalālayn's fifteen years for majority under al-Shāfiʿī he adds eighteen under Mālik, as al-Ṣāwī does. Allah fixed the shares Himself so that no heir would bear enmity toward the Prophet, an argument Ḥaqqī quotes from al-Taʾwīlāt al-najmiyyah. Beside the outward inheritance stands the spiritual inheritance of the ulama. Only two prohibitions in Q. 4:22–23 carry the exception "what has already passed", because both practices occurred among the Prophet's forefathers, and the exception protects his honour. The Jalālayn, al-Ṣāwī, Ḥaqqī and al-Rāzī explain it by pardon or by the force of the ban. None of them, nor al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Khāzin or Ibn ʿAjībah, ties it to his lineage.
10.author: A.K.

body: Shaykh Ibrāhīm completes the fourteen or fifteen women forbidden in marriage with the married woman (Q. 4:24), and separates permanent prohibitions from temporary ones. On Q. 4:25 he gives Mālik's two conditions for marrying a slave woman: the man cannot marry a free woman, and he fears hardship. He credits al-Shāfiʿī with reading nikāḥ as intercourse and stipulating nothing. Al-Bayḍāwī and al-Rāzī tie that reading to Abū Ḥanīfa, and the Jalālayn gloss he reads next puts al-Shāfiʿī with Mālik. Marriage is obligatory, recommended or forbidden according to a man's desire and means.

On Q. 4:26–28 he follows Ismāʿīl Ḥaqqī's Rūḥ al-bayān closely. Allah wishes four things for this community, whose journey runs by assistance (maʿūnah): Muḥammad ﷺ was carried by night, while Ibrāhīm and Mūsā travelled by their own effort (muʾnah). Weakness keeps the human being from holding to one state, so he becomes the best or the worst of creation.

At Q. 4:29 he tells of ʿĪsā, a Jew and a stolen loaf, to show what this world does to its children. On Q. 4:32 he takes al-Rāzī's three felicities, of soul, body and fortune. Envy wishes another's blessing gone. Emulation (ghibṭah) wishes for its like and is no sin, yet with al-Rāzī's "verifiers" he forbids asking for it. He treats the rebellious wife and the two arbiters (Q. 4:34–35), the intercession that brings believers out of the Fire, Muḥammad's community testifying for Nūḥ and the stages of the prohibition of wine. On dry ablution he sets the Jalālayn's "pure dust", al-Shāfiʿī's reading, beside Mālik's whole face of the earth, with the Shāfiʿī proof from Q. 7:58 that al-Qurṭubī reports.

Waḥshī's letters, told as in Rūḥ al-bayān, introduce Q. 4:48. The Murjiʾah hold that sin does a believer no harm. The Khawārij, as al-Bayḍāwī names them here, hold that a grave sin puts a Muslim out of Islam and into the Fire. Shaykh Ibrāhīm sides with the Ahl al-Sunnah: the grave sinner who dies unrepentant remains a Muslim, and Allah either forgives him or punishes him and admits him to the Garden. He treats the envy and miserliness of the Jews and outward and inward dominion, names three trusts, binds the believer to the Prophet's judgement (Q. 4:58–65) and closes with returning the greeting of peace (Q. 4:86).
11.author: A.K.

topics: The three ranks of the Prophet
Consensus and the kinds of shirk
body: Shaykh Ibrāhīm divides the Resurrection sworn in Q. 4:87 into the three of Ismāʿīl Ḥaqqī's Rūḥ al-bayān: the lesser is a person's death, the middle the death of all creatures at the first blast, the greater the raising at the second. On Q. 4:88 he sets out the positions on human acts in Ḥaqqī's terms. The Jabriyyah deny the servant any act and so abolish the legal obligations. The Qadariyyah make the servant the creator of his acts. The Ahl al-Sunnah hold "a small compulsion", Ḥaqqī's "middle compulsion": Allah gives the servant power to acquire and creates the deed at the moment of acquisition. The recognizers witness no agent but Allah, which Ḥaqqī too denies is compulsion, yet work as though they created their own deeds. He makes them a third way that joins the two errant creeds and draws pure milk from between dung and blood.

ʿAyyāsh b. Abī Rabīʿah's killing of al-Ḥārith, unaware of his conversion, occasions Q. 4:92 on killing by mistake. Emigration ended at the conquest of Mecca only as a condition of faith. Emigration itself never ends, and Allah completes the work of anyone who dies intending it.

The prayer of fear brings the story of Ghawrath and the reduction of fifty prayers to five. Ṭuʿmah b. Ubayriq's theft frames Q. 4:105–113. Al-Rāzī's "verifiers" take Q. 4:105 to deny the Prophet ﷺ ijtihād. Shaykh Ibrāhīm affirms it and concludes, with Ḥaqqī, that "his ijtihād is revelation". He explains the Prophet's clouding (ghayn), with al-Ṣāwī, as a covering of lights at each ascent, and gives him three ranks: a small rank, which is his share in the reward of all teaching, a middling rank known only to him, and a great rank known only to Allah.

Where the Jalālayn reads the "other way" of Q. 4:115 as unbelief, he derives from it the authority of consensus, as al-Rāzī reports al-Shāfiʿī did. With Ḥaqqī at Q. 4:48 he divides shirk into manifest, hidden and most hidden (seeing what is other than Allah) and denies forgiveness to all three. Al-Ṣāwī counts the hidden shirk of show among forgivable sins. He recounts ʿUmar's question about the most fearsome āyah (Q. 4:123), Sawdah's settlement (Q. 4:128) and ʿAlī's testament, and ends with the seven levels of the Fire, the hypocrites in al-Hāwiyah.
12.author: A.K.

topics: ʿĪsā and the seal of walāyah
body: Shaykh Ibrāhīm begins with Q. 4:148 and its occasion, a man reviling Abū Bakr in the Prophet's assembly. He takes from Ismāʿīl Ḥaqqī's Rūḥ al-bayān a three-level reading of the prohibition: the common people may not utter evil aloud, the elect may not voice it within the soul, and the elect of the elect may not let it cross the mind.

The Jews claimed to have killed ʿĪsā, though Allah had cast his likeness upon Ṭaṭyānūs, named by al-Ṣāwī (at Q. 3:54) and Ḥaqqī but not by the Jalālayn. At Q. 4:159, where the Jalālayn first refers "before his death" to the dying Jew or Christian, he refers it to ʿĪsā, as al-Ṭabarī preferred. ʿĪsā, whose spirit stood next to the spirit of Muḥammad in pre-eternity, will descend as a following walī, not an independent prophet, and as the seal of Muḥammadan walāyah. Ḥaqqī calls him the seal of absolute walāyah. All the major sins spring from three roots: following caprice, love of this world and seeing what is other than Allah.

At Q. 4:164 he rejects as very weak the report of eight thousand prophets, which al-Ṣāwī says al-Suyūṭī disowned. Al-Ṣāwī and Ḥaqqī leave the number unknown because the reports are weak. He argues from the names: each divine name manifests itself in a prophet, so only Allah knows their number. Mūsā heard Allah's speech without letter or sound. Al-Rāzī and al-Ṣāwī read Q. 4:165 against the Muʿtazilah. He grants that reason knows the world has a Maker but cannot apprehend a shariʿah without a prophet.

Al-Marwazī answers al-Rashīd's Christian physician, who took "a spirit from Him" (Q. 4:171) to make ʿĪsā part of Allah, by citing Q. 45:13, where everything in the heavens and the earth is likewise "from Him". Rūḥ al-bayān supplies the story. He adds that the spirit breathed into ʿĪsā came from the spirit of Muḥammad ﷺ. Allah Himself divided the shares of inheritance so that no heir would bear a grudge against the Prophet ﷺ.

Sūrat al-Māʾidah opens with al-Naqqāsh, whose attempt to match the Qurʾan ended at Q. 5:1. He treats divining arrows, the revelation of Q. 5:3 during the Farewell Pilgrimage, and the rulings on food, marriage and ablution, and ends with the Children of Isrāʾīl refusing to enter the holy land.
13.author: A.K.

topics: The Children of Isrāʾīl in the wilderness
The knowledge given to the Prophet
body: Shaykh Ibrāhīm begins with Yūshaʿ b. Nūn and Kālib b. Yūqannā, the chiefs who told only Mūsā and Hārūn what they had seen and trusted Allah's promise of the holy land. Al-Rāzī reports a dispute over whether Mūsā and Hārūn shared the people's forty years in the wilderness. Shaykh Ibrāhīm holds, with Rūḥ al-bayān, that they did, unharmed, as the fire was cool for Ibrāhīm, and draws Ḥaqqī's lesson of companionship.

After Hābīl, Qābīl and the crow, at Q. 5:33 he follows the Jalālayn's four cases of highway robbery, the ordering of Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Shāfiʿī, and reads banishment as imprisonment, since a robber sent elsewhere harms another town: the argument al-Rāzī reports from Abū Ḥanīfah. Mālik, al-Ṣāwī records, lets the imam choose the penalty and rejects prison as banishment. On theft, a Jew asked why a hand worth five hundred dīnārs in blood-money is cut off for a quarter dīnār: trust made it dear, treachery cheap.

From Q. 5:45 he sets Mālik, for whom the prescribed punishments restore the offender and expiate the sin, against al-Shāfiʿī, for whom they deter others while the sin remains, and sides with Mālik through the hadith of al-Ghāmidiyyah, whom the Prophet ﷺ called good after her stoning. Al-Qurṭubī reports al-Shāfiʿī as holding that the punishments are expiations. He recounts the stoning case at Khaybar, the apostasies under the Prophet, Abū Bakr and ʿUmar, and the origin of the call to prayer.

At Q. 5:64 the later scholars read Allah's hand as His power. Al-Rāzī and al-Ṣāwī object that power is one while the āyah gives two hands, and answer, as the Jalālayn glosses, that the dual conveys abundant generosity. Shaykh Ibrāhīm reads the gloss, presses the objection, and with the salaf leaves the hand in its outward sense and consigns its meaning to Allah, since His hand is not a bodily limb. From al-Ṣāwī he takes three kinds of knowledge given to the Prophet ﷺ: knowledge he had to convey, knowledge he was free to convey to the elect, and knowledge he had to conceal. Where al-Ṣāwī speaks of secrets, he names the second what the majādhīb utter in sheer annihilation, and the third the secret of the decree. He recounts how Būlus split the followers of ʿĪsā and ends at Q. 5:81.
14.author: A.K.

topics: The messengers' reply at the Resurrection
The table of ʿĪsā and the three feasts
body: At Q. 5:82 Shaykh Ibrāhīm takes al-Rāzī's point: Christian unbelief is grosser than Jewish, touching divinity and prophethood where the Jews' touches prophethood alone. Yet the Jews show the Muslims greater enmity, because their love of this world breeds envy, arrogance and love of leadership. The Jalālayn ties the āyah to the Negus's delegation, and al-Rāzī reports Ibn ʿAbbās confining it there. Shaykh Ibrāhīm, with Rūḥ al-bayān and Ibn ʿAjībah, extends it to all priests and monks.
He tells the Muslims' case before the Negus largely as al-Ṣāwī does, and adds how ʿAmr b. al-ʿĀṣ brought ʿUmārah b. al-Walīd to ruin, a story absent from the commentaries he worked from.

At Q. 5:87 ʿUthmān b. Maẓʿūn and his companions resolve to renounce meat, perfume, sleep and marriage, and the Prophet ﷺ forbids it. With al-Rāzī, he reads the āyah as a check on the praise just given to monks. Monasticism weakens the body and with it the intellect, while indulgence drowns a person in this world. Both bar the way to recognition, the goal.

On the expiation of oaths, Mālik and al-Shāfiʿī require a measure of grain handed to each of the ten poor, while Abū Ḥanīfah accepts a midday and an evening meal. Shaykh Ibrāhīm sides with the first two and reverses the Ḥanafī reading al-Rāzī reports: «what you feed your families» means making food over, not setting it before them. He treats wine, hunting in iḥrām and the camels the pagans dedicated to idols.

He calls Q. 5:106 the most difficult āyah in its grammar, meaning and ruling, with al-Ṣāwī, al-Rāzī and al-Qurṭubī, and explains it through Tamīm al-Dārī and the silver goblet. At Q. 5:109 the Jalālayn says terror wipes out the messengers' knowledge. He answers, with al-Rāzī and Q. 21:103, that they leave the knowledge to Allah out of adab. He recounts ʿĪsā's table, explains that the three feasts of Friday, the Breaking of the Fast and the Sacrifice mark the completion of prayer, fasting and hajj, and draws out ʿĪsā's adab in Q. 5:116–118.

Sūrat al-Anʿām is Meccan and came down all at once. Meccan surahs are more concise because they addressed Quraysh, while Medinan surahs expand for the Jews. He sets out the inimitability of the Qurʾan and ends at Q. 6:35.
15.author: A.K.

topics: The hierarchy of spirit, intellect and recognition
body: Shaykh Ibrāhīm begins at Q. 6:36, where Allah calls the unbelievers dead. The spirit gives life to the body, the intellect to the spirit, and recognition to the intellect. Whoever lacks all three is dead.

He rejects the claim that the Prophet ﷺ had no miracles: the Qurʾan alone holds more than two thousand, since the challenge is a single surah of three āyāt, as al-Rāzī reckons. At Q. 6:38 the Jalālayn takes the Book to be the Preserved Tablet. Shaykh Ibrāhīm adds al-Rāzī's reading, the Qurʾan, and its limit to religion, then drops the limit: everything is in the Qurʾan. He cites al-Shāfiʿī and a boy in Rabat who silenced a Christian.

The Ashʿarīs and most theologians, Rūḥ al-bayān reports, cite Q. 6:50 to deny the Prophet ﷺ ijtihād. Al-Rāzī adds Q. 53:3–4. Shaykh Ibrāhīm holds, with Rūḥ al-bayān and Q. 4:105, that he did, and that his ijtihād is itself revelation, so both parties speak truly. He affirms analogy against its deniers. He recounts the occasion of Q. 6:52 and the People of the Bench.

Al-Ṣāwī treats the five matters of Q. 31:34 alike. Shaykh Ibrāhīm, nearer Rūḥ al-bayān at that āyah, sets one apart: only the coming of the Hour belongs to Allah alone. The awliyāʾ who foretell the other four do so through Allah's knowledge, and Shaykh Aḥmad al-Tijānī said he could tell all five even after burial. He discusses the Pen and the Trumpet.

He rejects the answer that the Prophet's ﷺ forefathers were kept from shirk only while his light was in their loins, and prefers al-Tijānī's reading that Āzar was Ibrāhīm's paternal uncle, a view al-Ṣāwī reports and al-Rāzī rejects. He recounts Ibrāhīm's hidden birth. The Jalālayn, al-Ṣāwī and al-Rāzī read "This is my Lord" as a move in debate with his people. He reads it as the words of one passed away in tawḥīd, who meant his real Lord and then returned to sobriety. Ibn ʿAjībah's ishārah, that Ibrāhīm saw Allah in all things, comes nearest.

He distinguishes false security before Allah's scheme from the security of faith unmixed with shirk. The Prophet ﷺ was commanded to follow all the prophets because he gathers their dispersed virtues. He recounts how Abū Bakr and ʿUthmān collected the Qurʾan, and ends at Q. 6:110.
16.author: A.K.

topics: Faith by Allah's will, not by signs
Occasions of revelation in a surah revealed at once
Q. 6:119 and the later Sūrat al-Māʾidah
body: Shaykh Ibrāhīm begins with Q. 6:111. Sūrat al-Anʿām came down all at once, so assigning an occasion of revelation to one of its āyāt is hard. With Rūḥ al-bayān, he holds that faith comes by Allah's will, not by signs: even the Resurrection, the greatest sign, would not bring the deniers to faith (Q. 6:28).

He explains why every prophet has an enemy and, after Ismāʿīl Ḥaqqī, why animals are slaughtered in Allah's name: the sweetness of His name takes away the bitterness of death. The Jalālayn refers Q. 6:119 to Q. 5:3, revealed later. Al-Rāzī and Ḥaqqī prefer Q. 6:145. Shaykh Ibrāhīm keeps Q. 5:3 because in Allah's presence there is no past or future. After Q. 6:127 a queen embraces Islam at the Prophet's grave.

At Q. 6:128 he finds the Jalālayn's readings of "except as Allah wills" unsatisfactory. His answer turns on the name al-Ākhir, which must be manifested. The people of the Garden rise in bliss until they become absent in it, and the people of the Fire grow used to their pain until they no longer feel it. Both return in post-eternity to their state in pre-eternity, yet remain forever in their abodes. The resolution follows Ḥaqqī's shaykh in Rūḥ al-bayān, down to the lost feeling, the pre-eternal state and the intervening trials. None of nine commentaries, from al-Ṭabarī to Ibn ʿAjībah, argues from al-Ākhir.

He recounts how Quraysh divided crops and cattle and a father's confession that he had killed his daughter. At Q. 6:148, with the Jalālayn and al-Ṣāwī, he grants the associators that Allah willed their shirk and denies that He is therefore content with it. They measured Allah by the creature, who wills only what benefits him. Allah wills unbelief without being content with it.

He sets out the ten prohibitions of Q. 6:151–153 and traces every prohibition back to killing. At Q. 6:160 he corrects the Jalālayn, which limits "the good deed" to lā ilāha illā Llāh: every good deed counts. With Rūḥ al-bayān, good deeds multiply as they rise from the heart to the spirit to the secret, as units become tens, hundreds and thousands, while evil deeds stay in the soul and count once. He ends at Q. 6:165 calling Muslims back to the Book of Allah.
17.author: A.K.
